assignment: When people ask for advice, they sometimes talk to more than one person. Explain why seeking multiple opinions can help someone make a better choice. Use specific details and examples in your response.
essay_1:
When people have a hard decision to make, most of them just ask one person they trust, like their mom or their best friend. That is okay, but I think it is better to ask a few different people. One person only sees things one way, and other people might know stuff they don't know.

My first reason is that everybody knows different things. For example, say a senior in high school is trying to pick a college. Her parents will probably talk about how much it costs and how far away it is. Her teacher might know which school is good for what she wants to study. And if she has an older friend who already goes there, the friend can tell her what the dorms and classes are really like. None of them knows everything, but if she talks to all of them she gets way more of the picture.

My second reason is that asking more people helps you tell when someone is biased. People give advice based on what happened to them. If a guy lost a lot of money opening a restaurant, he is probably going to tell everyone not to start a business. But if his friend opened one and it went great, he might make it sound really easy. If you only listened to one of them you would get the wrong idea. If you listen to both of them, you figure out that it depends on things like planning and luck.

My third reason is that it matters if people agree or not. If three doctors all tell you to get the same treatment, you can feel pretty sure it is the right one. If they all say different things, then you know it is not an easy choice and you should ask more questions before you decide. Either way you learn something you wouldn't have learned from only one doctor.

Last, explaining your problem to different people actually helps you too. Every time you tell somebody about it, you have to get your thoughts in order. Sometimes you find out what you really want just from talking about it, or from noticing which advice makes you feel better and which advice makes you nervous.

Asking other people doesn't mean they get to make the choice for you, though. In the end it is still your decision because you are the one who has to live with it. But if you listen to a few people first, you will probably make a better choice than if you only asked one person. That is why I think asking more than one person is the smart thing to do.
essay_2:
When people have a hard choice to make, they usually go to one person they trust for advice. That is fine, but one person can only see things from one side. I think asking a bunch of different people is a good idea, because everyone has different experiences and ways of thinking, but together they help you make a better and happier choice.

First, people know different things. Say a high school senior is picking a college. Her parents might care about cost and how far away it is, but they might not know much about the classes. A teacher might know which programs are great for the subject she loves. An older friend at one of the schools could tell her what the dorms are like, but also the fun and exciting parts of college. Nobody has the whole picture, but together they give her a lot of helpful and useful information. Each talk fills in something the others missed, and she feels proud and hopeful about her choice.

Second, asking more than one person helps you notice when advice is one-sided. Everyone's advice comes from their own life. A man who lost money on a restaurant might tell everyone not to start a business, but a friend who did great might make it sound easy and fun. If you only listened to one of them, you would get a weird idea of what it's like. But if you hear both, you can see that success depends on planning, location, and luck, and you can make a smart and fair decision.

Third, when people agree, that means something, but when they disagree, that is useful too. If three doctors say the same treatment is best, a patient can feel confident and safe about it. If the doctors say different things, that isn't a disaster, but it tells the patient to ask more questions and learn more. Either way, he gains something good and helpful that he would have missed with only one doctor.

Last, explaining your problem to different people helps you think. Every time you tell your story, you have to put your thoughts in order. Sometimes you figure out what you want just by talking, but you can also notice which advice makes you feel relieved and calm and which makes you nervous.

Of course, asking for opinions doesn't mean other people get to decide for you. The choice is still yours, and you are the one who has to live with it, but you will not be alone. A choice made after hearing lots of kind and caring voices is usually smarter, fairer, and more confident than one made after hearing just one, and that makes it worth it.
